stages.P1: What real people would answer about the product or category: answer distributions by segment, with reasons
stages.P2: First impression and preference from the page or demo, before use: shares across product and competitors, perception ratings, reasons
stages.P3: Preference after attempting given tasks: who completes, where they fail, post-task preference, why
stages.P4: Which product people would choose overall (primary): choice shares by segment, explained by P1-P3

unknown_products.label: Unknown products
unknown_products.desc: Products or stimuli a model cannot know the outcome for ('no brand to lean on')

competitors.label: Competitors in one judgement
competitors.desc: People judge or choose between alternatives, so shares across products can be scored

headroom.label: Harness headroom
headroom.desc: A bare frontier model sits well below the noise ceiling, so harness gains are visible

public_arm.label: Fair public-data arm
public_arm.desc: Outside public evidence exists that a harness may use without leaking the answer

target_pop.label: Target population
target_pop.desc: Segment attributes, or each person's own source data (history, interviews, behaviour)

heldout_same.label: Held-out outcomes, same people
heldout_same.desc: New questions, studies or later behaviour for the same people or segments

reasons.label: Reasons
reasons.desc: Multi-dimension ratings, rationales or free text

tasks.label: Tasks with outcomes
tasks.desc: Given tasks with completion and failure points (P3)

baseline.label: Accepted baseline
baseline.desc: A published bare-model or standard baseline, so others accept the comparison

power.label: Statistical power
power.desc: Enough people, items or studies to detect a +1-2 point gain

digital.label: Digital-product realism
digital.desc: Digital products comparable to a startup's

license.label: Publishable
license.desc: Licence or terms allow publishing results

status.restricted: Restricted: on request, data deal, or non-commercial terms
status.proposed: Proposed: needs a pipeline or new data collection

benchmarks.name: Twin-2K-500 Mega-Study

P1.why: 19 new pre-registered studies, 164 outcomes, answered by the same 1,784 Twin-2K people: person-level, held out

P2.why: Some studies rate new stimuli before use (idea evaluation, NFT luxury goods, ad targeting)

P4.why: Context and default-effect choices; not products against competitors

benchmarks.note: Published bar: twins correlate r = 0.20-0.23 with individuals and are no more accurate than demographics-only personas (0.748 vs 0.746). Answers too uniform on 154 of 164 outcomes.

benchmarks.name: Twin-2K-500

P1.why: 500+ answers per person, 2,058 people, retest wave: person-level distributions with a ceiling

P2.why: Product description plus price, then buy or not

P4.why: Buy yes/no at a price; no competitor

benchmarks.note: Branded groceries. Our adapter: reasons axes beat demographics (TVD 0.480 vs 0.490; group-gap correlation 0.44 vs 0.10); segments unstable.

benchmarks.name: PRISM
benchmarks.license: CC BY 4.0 text; CC BY-NC 4.0 model responses

P1.why: Profile survey of 1,500 people with stated preferences about AI, by segment

P2.why: First-turn ratings of up to 4 models before choosing; several conversations per person (LoRe: 62.5% -> 71.0% with about 4 examples per user)

P4.why: Per-conversation choice; no overall adoption decision

unverified: unknown_products: whether models were anonymous to participants
benchmarks.note: The only public set linking profiles, free-text self-descriptions, first impressions and choice for the same people.

benchmarks.name: OPeRA

P1.why: Persona surveys and optional 20-minute interviews of 51 shoppers

P3.why: About 13 real sessions per person over 4 weeks: every action, purchase or abandon, rationale per step; later sessions can be held out

P4.why: Purchase among products found

benchmarks.note: The only open set with interview, survey and behaviour for the same people. Prompted GPT-4.1 21.5% next action; SFT+RL about 38-40%.

benchmarks.name: SimBench

P1.why: 20 datasets of real group answer distributions; held-out questions per group

benchmarks.note: Our strongest proof that harness + public data beats the bare model: 41.5 -> 55.8 with no target labels. Group level only.

benchmarks.name: Pew ATP tech adoption
benchmarks.license: Free account; no resale or redistribution

P1.why: Person-level answers with demographics; the same panelists across waves

P4.why: Which platforms people use (big brands)

benchmarks.note: Download requires a Pew account.

benchmarks.name: Community Alignment

P1.why: Survey of 15k nationally representative people in 5 countries

P2.why: Preferences among response variants, with annotator demographics

P4.why: Choice among variants of one model, not products

benchmarks.note: Over 200k comparisons from 3,500 annotators.

benchmarks.name: HUMAINE

P1.why: Goal and engagement scores are labels from a GPT-4.1 judge, not answers from people

P3.why: Post-use comparison after people's own tasks, but no human completion labels

P4.why: Choice shares by segment exist, but the LMArena ratings alone predict them as well as our best model (45.9 vs 45.8); per-vote age effects are nil. Tie rates are people-dependent

benchmarks.note: Products are famous AI models with public leaderboards. Our run: Gemini 23.2 -> 39.5 with arena ratings; ceiling 71.8. Useful for tie/indifference behaviour and pilot-calibration tests.

benchmarks.name: Miniukovich & Figl homepages

P1.why: Rating distributions by demographic and domain familiarity

P2.why: About 3,150 homepages rated by 2,822 people on aesthetics, trust, usability and prototypicality, with rate-rerate duplicates

benchmarks.note: Best free first-impression set with segments (banking, shopping, university sites).

benchmarks.name: LabInTheWild web appeal

P1.why: Appeal distributions by demographic and country

P2.why: 500 ms first impressions of website screenshots, 40k+ people

benchmarks.note: Demographics move the preference peak but explain little variance.

benchmarks.name: Upworthy A/B archive

P2.why: Click shares across headline variants: first impression of a message, aggregate

P4.why: A click is a micro-choice

benchmarks.note: 32,487 randomized tests. Raw LLMs recover 39% of the effect; tree calibration closes it (Spotify).

benchmarks.name: WiserUI-Bench

P2.why: Real UI A/B pairs with the winning variant

P4.why: Variant that converted better

benchmarks.note: 300 pairs; frontier models near chance once order is controlled.

benchmarks.name: ConvApparel

P3.why: Shopping task with a randomized good or bad recommender; turn-level satisfaction and frustration, post-session survey

P4.why: Which assistant served better, by condition

benchmarks.note: Best public test of whether a simulator moves in the right direction under a product change.

benchmarks.name: Hillstrom / X5 uplift

P4.why: Purchase after a randomized campaign, per customer with purchase history

benchmarks.note: Customer history plus a randomized intervention; tabular, not clickstream.

benchmarks.name: Park et al. 1,000 interviews

P1.why: 2-hour interviews, then new survey answers two weeks later, scored against each person's retest

P4.why: Economic games, not product choice

unverified: whether the restricted API has opened
benchmarks.note: The exact interview-to-twin design: 0.83-0.86 of retest vs 0.74 for demographics. Methods template; apply for research access.

benchmarks.name: Chatbot Arena votes

P2.why: Blind first-turn votes, largely predictable from model quality

P4.why: Blind pairwise votes between famous products

benchmarks.note: Huge volume, no demographics.

benchmarks.name: Kickstarter
benchmarks.license: public file lacks page text; text file restricted

P4.why: Backing with real money among new, unknown products

benchmarks.note: 610k projects 2009-2023; mostly physical and creative products.

benchmarks.name: Show HN (live)

P2.why: Landing-page first impression of real new startups, aggregate

P3.why: Some comments come from people who tried the product

P4.why: Upvotes measure interest, not adoption

benchmarks.note: Live, so nothing to memorize; needs the forecasting pipeline.

benchmarks.name: Product Hunt (live)

P4.why: Daily ranking among the day's launches

benchmarks.note: Campaign noise in rankings.

benchmarks.name: G2 / Capterra reviews
benchmarks.license: no scraping; needs a data deal

P3.why: Post-use ease of use, setup, support

P4.why: Alternatives considered and switched from

benchmarks.note: Closest to B2B software choice, but not usable without a licence.

benchmarks.name: App store reviews

P4.why: Rating as a weak proxy for choice

benchmarks.note: No demographics.

benchmarks.name: ShopCART

P3.why: 31,865 Amazon sessions with actions and outcomes

P4.why: Purchase or not

benchmarks.note: Authors say they cannot release the data.

benchmarks.name: Online-Mind2Web

P3.why: Task completion on real websites; no preference

benchmarks.note: Task mechanics (branch 3), not preference.

benchmarks.name: Anthropic Interviewer

P1.why: 1,250 interview transcripts about AI at work; no structured held-out outcomes

benchmarks.note: Realistic interview text for testing ingestion and PII handling; nothing to predict.

benchmarks.name: UserSim own panel (target design)

P1.why: Profile survey of the same people

P2.why: First impression of product and competitors' pages

P3.why: The same people attempt the same tasks on each product

P4.why: Then choose

benchmarks.note: Not collected. The only design that links P1-P4 for the same people on unknown products.
